name: Zephyr
vendor: Zephyr Project (Linux Foundation), based on Wind River’s Rocket kernel

foundation.via: A member-funded Linux Foundation project with its own governing board and technical steering committee

summary: A real-time operating system for microcontrollers: the firmware on the sensor, wearable or controller at the edge of an IoT system, with its own networking, Bluetooth and MQTT client, built for more than 1,000 boards.
intro: In an IoT system, Zephyr is the software on the device. It is a small real-time kernel for microcontrollers and other resource-constrained hardware, from environmental sensors and LED wearables to smart watches and embedded controllers, compiled together with your application into a single firmware image. Kconfig options choose which subsystems go in and how big their buffers are, and devicetree describes the board’s hardware, so the image holds only what the application uses. It supports Arm Cortex-M, -R and -A, RISC-V, x86, ARC and Xtensa, plus Hexagon, MIPS, SPARC, TriCore and a few others, on more than 1,000 boards. The kernel offers preemptive and cooperative threads, an earliest-deadline-first scheduler option, semaphores, message queues and power management, plus memory protection and user-mode threads on Arm, x86 and ARC.

Connectivity is in the tree rather than bolted on: a native IP stack with BSD sockets, an MQTT client for MQTT 3.1.0, 3.1.1 and 5.0 over TCP or TLS, LwM2M for device management, OpenThread, Wi-Fi and a qualification-ready Bluetooth Low Energy host and controller with Mesh. So a Zephyr device is typically the client that keeps an MQTT connection open to a broker such as EMQX or AWS IoT Core. Around the kernel come file systems (LittleFS, FAT, ext2), key-value settings in flash, logging and an interactive shell. The `west` tool fetches Zephyr and its modules, such as vendor hardware layers, then builds and flashes; `native_sim` runs the same application as a Linux process for testing.

Major releases come every six months, in April and October: 4.4.0 shipped on 14 April 2026, and 4.5 reached its third release candidate on 22 October 2026. A long-term-support release follows every 2.5 to 3 years and is maintained for about five years; the current one, 3.7 LTS from July 2024, is supported until July 2029, and the next is planned as 4.6 in April 2027. Chip makers build their SDKs on it: Nordic Semiconductor’s nRF Connect SDK, for example, is Zephyr plus Nordic’s libraries and drivers.
strengths: Vendor-neutral and broad: one RTOS, build system and driver model across more than 1,000 boards from many chip makers
Networking, Bluetooth LE, MQTT, LwM2M, TLS and file systems come with the kernel instead of being assembled from separate projects
Long-term-support releases maintained for about five years, with security fixes and an auditable branch aimed at certification
Apache 2.0, so device makers can ship firmware without publishing their own code
limits: More to learn than a bare scheduler: an application is shaped by Kconfig, devicetree overlays, CMake and `west` as much as by its C code
APIs keep changing between releases; each release has a migration guide, and a non-LTS release is supported for only about a year
A full workspace pulls in many modules and vendor hardware layers unless you limit them with project groups
An RTOS for microcontrollers: devices with an MMU that need full Linux processes, drivers and package managers are better served by embedded Linux

sections.title: Get the code, build for a board and flash it
sections.intro: From Zephyr’s getting-started guide; `west` creates a workspace from the zephyr repository’s manifest.
source: cd ~/zephyrproject && west update     # fetches Zephyr’s modules and vendor HALs
west flash                            # program the connected board
west build -p always -b native_sim samples/hello_world   # or run it as a Linux process

story: Zephyr’s kernel goes back to Virtuoso, a real-time OS for digital signal processors from the Belgian company Eonic Systems, which Wind River bought in 2001. In November 2015 Wind River renamed it Rocket and released it as open, royalty-free software for IoT devices; it could fit in as little as 4 KB of memory, where Wind River’s VxWorks needed 200 KB or more.

Linux itself was too big for the smallest IoT devices, so on 17 February 2016 the Linux Foundation launched the Zephyr Project around the Rocket kernel, backed by Intel (with Wind River and Altera), NXP, Synopsys and UbiquiOS. It started with four boards, including the Arduino 101 and NXP’s FRDM-K64F, and with Bluetooth, Bluetooth Low Energy and IEEE 802.15.4 networking. In December 2016, version 1.6 replaced the original nanokernel and microkernel split with a single kernel.

Chip makers and device companies joined as members, and Zephyr became one of the most active RTOS projects on GitHub. Long-term-support releases (1.14, 2.7 and 3.7 in July 2024) gave product makers a base to certify against, and the list of architectures kept growing, most recently with OpenRISC in 4.4 in April 2026. From 2026 the project moved to two major releases a year, in April and October.

choices.choice: Configured and sized at compile time
choices.why: On a microcontroller with a few kilobytes of RAM there is nothing to spare, so Kconfig and devicetree decide at build time which code and resources exist, and unused features cost nothing.

choices.choice: Hardware described as data, borrowed from Linux
choices.why: Devicetree describes each board’s peripherals in a file, so one driver serves every board with the same hardware block and the build includes only what the board has.

choices.choice: A permissive licence under a neutral foundation
choices.why: Apache 2.0 under the Linux Foundation lets competing chip makers contribute drivers to one RTOS while device makers keep their own firmware closed.

timeline.text: Wind River buys Eonic Systems, maker of the Virtuoso RTOS
Wind River releases Virtuoso as the open-source Rocket RTOS
Linux Foundation launches the Zephyr Project on 17 February; 1.6 moves to a single kernel in December
3.7, the third LTS release, ships in July
4.4 in April adds OpenRISC and Zephyr SDK 1.0; six-month release cadence begins
